A saying is a short, familiar phrase or sentence that expresses a general truth, a piece of wisdom, or a common observation about life. It is something many people know, repeat, and pass down — often across generations.

Think of it this way: human beings have been living, struggling, learning, and observing the world for thousands of years. Over time, they noticed patterns — certain things that tend to be true about life, people, and how the world works. They summed up these observations into short, memorable sentences. Those sentences are sayings.

• "Actions speak louder than words" — What a person does reveals more about them than what they say. A person who promises much but delivers little is exposed by this saying.
  • "Every cloud has a silver lining" — Even in a bad or painful situation, there is usually something positive to be found if you look carefully.
  • "Look before you leap" — Think carefully and consider the consequences before you make a decision or take a big step.
  • "The early bird catches the worm" — Those who start early, or act quickly, tend to get the best opportunities.
  • "Don't judge a book by its cover" — Don't form an opinion about something (or someone) based only on outward appearance.

Notice how each of these is just one sentence, yet each one carries a complete lesson about life.

1. It's short.
A saying is almost always a single sentence. It doesn't need paragraphs to explain itself — the whole point is that it's compact and easy to remember.

2. It's widely known.
A saying is not a private observation. It's shared — something that many people across a culture or society know and use. When you say "as the saying goes," the person listening already knows the phrase.

3. It expresses a general truth or observation.
It makes a statement about how life or human nature tends to work — not about one specific person or event, but about situations in general.

4. It applies broadly.
A saying is not tied to one moment in history. "Actions speak louder than words" applies equally to a politician in 1850 and a colleague in your office today. That timeless applicability is part of what makes something a saying.

5. It is often figurative.
Many sayings use a simple image to point to a deeper truth. "Every cloud has a silver lining" is not literally about weather — it's about finding hope in difficulty. "The early bird catches the worm" is not really about birds — it's about the advantage of acting early. This figurative quality is what makes sayings vivid and memorable.

You'll often see it introduced like this:

  • "There's an old saying: 'Don't count your chickens before they hatch.'"
  • "As the saying goes, 'better late than never.'"
  • "My grandfather had a saying for every occasion."
  • "She reminded me of that saying about not judging a book by its cover."

The plural "sayings" is also commonly used to refer to a collection of wise expressions attributed to a particular person:

  • "The sayings of Confucius have been studied for centuries."
  • "The sayings of the Buddha offer guidance on how to live."

Here, "sayings" refers to the notable, wise remarks that a person made — remarks so insightful that people recorded and repeated them.

The word saying is the broadest, most general term. Several related words refer to more specific types of sayings:

Proverb — A type of saying that is typically old, traditional, and often uses a metaphor or image to make its point. "Don't count your chickens before they hatch" (don't assume success before it happens). All proverbs are sayings, but not all sayings are proverbs.

Adage — Essentially the same as a proverb. An adage is an old, widely accepted piece of wisdom. "Haste makes waste" (rushing causes mistakes). The word "adage" simply emphasises that the saying is old and well-established.

Maxim — A short saying that states a rule of conduct or a guiding principle, often in a more formal or serious tone. "Treat others as you wish to be treated." Maxims tend to be prescriptive — they tell you how to behave.

Aphorism — A clever, insightful statement of a general truth, often made by a known individual. "To err is human; to forgive, divine" (Alexander Pope). Aphorisms are often more literary and witty, and are frequently attributed to a specific author or thinker.

Idiom — A phrase whose meaning is different from the literal meaning of its words. "It's raining cats and dogs" (it's raining heavily). An idiom can be a saying, but many idioms simply describe something colourfully rather than express wisdom or a life lesson.

In everyday conversation, people use all these words loosely and interchangeably. "Saying" is the safest and most common choice for all of them.
An important truth about sayings: they are not laws

Sayings express general tendencies — they are not meant to be absolute rules that hold true in every single situation without exception.

This is why some sayings appear to contradict each other:

  • "Look before you leap" → Think carefully before you act.
  • "He who hesitates is lost" → Don't wait too long, or you'll miss your chance.

Both are sayings. Both are wise. They simply apply to different kinds of situations. The first warns against recklessness; the second warns against excessive caution. This is not a flaw in sayings — it's a reflection of the genuine complexity of life. A saying is a tool, and like a tool, you use the right one for the right situation.

Sayings are powerful because they compress an entire life lesson into one short sentence. When someone says "Actions speak louder than words," there is no need to explain the whole idea — both people already know the saying, and the meaning lands instantly. This makes conversation faster, richer, and more colourful.

Sayings also carry authority without being preachy. When you give someone direct advice, it can feel like your personal opinion. But when you invoke a saying, it feels like the wisdom of many people across many years — which makes it harder to dismiss and easier to accept.

A saying is a short, widely known expression that captures a general truth or piece of wisdom about life. It is brief, memorable, and figurative. It applies broadly across situations and time. It is the umbrella term that includes proverbs, adages, maxims, and aphorisms. It is not a law — it is practical wisdom, and its value lies in how well you know when and where to apply it.
